---
title: "Committing, pushing, and pulling"
subtitle: "Guide 4 of 4 · every time you work"
---

## The mental model

Saving a file and saving your work are different things. Git puts three
checkpoints between the file on your disk and the copy on GitHub, and almost
every confusion about Git comes from collapsing them.

| Step | What it does | Where the work now is |
|---|---|---|
| **Save** (Ctrl/Cmd+S) | Writes your edits to the file | On your disk only |
| **Stage** (tick the box) | Marks a file as part of the next snapshot | Chosen, not yet recorded |
| **Commit** | Records a permanent snapshot with a message | In your local history |
| **Push** | Uploads your commits to GitHub | On GitHub, visible to others |

The consequence worth memorizing: **a commit is not on GitHub until you push.**
Every term, someone commits diligently all week, never pushes, and believes the
work was submitted. Only what is pushed exists to anyone but you.

**Pull** is the reverse of push: it brings down commits made elsewhere (by a
collaborator, by your other laptop, or by an edit you made on github.com in the
browser).

## The routine

Once your project is open in RStudio, you will use the **Git** tab in the
top-right pane. Files appear there as soon as they change.

### 1. Pull before you start

Click the blue **Pull** arrow. If you are the only person working, this usually
reports "Already up to date", which takes a second and saves you the rejected
push described below.

### 2. Do your work, and save

Nothing Git-related here. Edit, save, run, render.

### 3. Stage what belongs in this snapshot

In the Git tab, tick the **Staged** checkbox next to each file you want to
include. The two-letter status codes mean:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `M` | Modified: the file existed and you changed it |
| `A` | Added: a new file, now staged |
| `?` | Untracked: a new file Git has never seen (`git status` calls it `??`) |
| `D` | Deleted |
| `R` | Renamed |

Stage your source files. Do not stage things that are generated, huge, or
private: see [what not to commit](#what-not-to-commit).

### 4. Commit

Click **Commit**. A window opens showing your staged changes line by line, with
additions in green and deletions in red. Read that diff: it is the cheapest bug
check you will ever get.

Write a message in the box and click **Commit**.

A good message says what changed and why, in the present tense, in one line:

- Good: `Add Q3 boxplot and fix filter on year`
- Good: `Correct sample size in the summary table`
- Less useful: `update`, `stuff`, `asdf`, `final FINAL v2`

You are writing to your future self, who will scroll this history in three
months looking for the commit where something broke.

### 5. Push

Close the commit window and click the green **Push** arrow. When it finishes,
your work is on GitHub.

If Push asks for a username and password, your token is not set up: go back to
[guide 2](github-setup.qmd). If it reports that updates were rejected, click
**Pull** first, then Push again.

### 6. Confirm

Open the repository on github.com and look at it. Your files should be there,
with your commit message and a timestamp beside them. This takes five seconds
and is the only real proof that the work is submitted.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In this course

After you push, click the **Actions** tab on your repository page. Within about
two minutes the autograder reports which questions passed. You can revise and
push as often as you like before the deadline: only the final state counts, so a
red X on an early attempt costs you nothing.
:::

## What not to commit {#what-not-to-commit}

Git is for source, not for output or secrets.

| Do commit | Do not commit |
|---|---|
| `.R` and `.qmd` files | Tokens, passwords, API keys |
| Small input data | Data you are not allowed to redistribute |
| `.gitignore`, `README.md`, `.Rproj` | Files over 100 MB (GitHub refuses them) |
| Anything needed to reproduce the work | `.Rproj.user/`, `.Rhistory`, `.RData` |

A `.gitignore` file lists patterns Git should ignore, so those files stop
appearing in the Git tab entirely. RStudio creates a sensible one for you when it
makes a project. To add to it:

```r
usethis::use_git_ignore(c("*.csv", "secrets.R"))
```

::: {.callout-important}
Committing a secret and then deleting it does not remove it: it stays in the
history and is still readable. If you push a token or password, revoke it
immediately on GitHub and issue a new one. That is the fix; editing the file is
not.
:::

## The same thing in the Terminal

The Git tab is a friendly front end for a handful of commands. If you prefer typing, or
you are on a machine without RStudio, these are the equivalents. Run them in the
RStudio **Terminal** tab or any shell, from inside the project folder.

```bash
git status                        # what has changed, and what is staged
git add exercise.qmd              # stage one file
git add .                         # stage everything changed
git commit -m "Add Q3 boxplot"    # record a snapshot
git push                          # upload to GitHub
git pull                          # download from GitHub
git log --oneline                 # your history, one commit per line
```

`git status` is the single most useful command in Git. When you are lost, run
it: it tells you where you are and usually suggests the command you want next.

## Undoing things

Nothing here loses committed work. Git makes it genuinely hard to destroy
something you have committed, which is most of the point of using it.

| You want to | In RStudio | In the Terminal |
|---|---|---|
| Unstage a file | Untick its Staged box | `git restore --staged FILE` |
| Throw away uncommitted edits to a file | Git tab > select > More > Revert | `git restore FILE` |
| Fix the message on the last commit | Commit window > tick **Amend previous commit** | `git commit --amend` |
| See what changed in a file | Git tab > select > Diff | `git diff FILE` |
| Look at an old version | Git tab > History (clock icon) | `git log -p FILE` |

::: {.callout-warning}
Reverting uncommitted changes is the one genuinely destructive action in that
table. Those edits were never recorded, so Git cannot bring them back. Commit
first when you are unsure: a messy commit is always better than lost work.
:::

Only amend a commit you have not pushed yet. Amending rewrites history, and
rewriting history that others have already pulled creates a mess for them.

## When two people edit the same lines

If you and a collaborator change the same lines of the same file, a pull
produces a **merge conflict**. Git marks the disagreement inside the file:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
mean_age <- mean(df$age, na.rm = TRUE)
=======
mean_age <- mean(df$age)
>>>>>>> origin/main
```

To resolve it: open the file, delete the three marker lines, keep the code you
want (which may be a blend of both), save, then stage and commit as usual. The
commit that follows is the resolution.

Conflicts are normal collaboration, not a failure. They are also much rarer when
everyone pulls before starting and pushes when they finish.
